scenario: AITA for not buying my siblings gifts because they refuse to do a secret Santa? | I have a bunch of siblings, all grown adults, and buying gifts for everyone including parents, partners, and kids is out of control. While I am financially okish, I just can't afford it. Also, neither can my parents and previous years have resulted in my mom being depressed and stressed trying to buy everyone something. Last year, after a some resistance, we agreed to do a secret santa and it went pretty well. Or so I thought. This year 1 sibling threw a fit about doing it. She said she doesn't like "putting rules on holidays" and it's not fair. As a side note, she and our younger siblings rarely buy anyone anything. Last year was the 1st time everyone brought something. Another sibling, who is hosting Christmas, sided with her and said that we won't do a secret Santa but that you don't have to bring gifts if you don't want to. Am an asshole if I don't buy my siblings gifts? I love my family but I can't afford it this year. I was going to get nieces and nephews gifts but that's it.

message.reasoning:
Hmm, let's break this down. The user is asking whether it's morally acceptable to not buy gifts for siblings after a Secret Santa agreement fell apart due to one sibling's resistance. The core issue seems to be financial strain and fairness. 

The person can't afford gifts for everyone, and the family previously agreed to Secret Santa to reduce stress and cost. Now, one sibling is refusing, which disrupts the system. The user is considering only buying for nieces/nephews, which aligns with the original intent of reducing financial burden. 

Morally, it seems reasonable to prioritize financial stability and follow through on a collective agreement that was meant to help everyone. The sibling who objected is being inconsistent—previously accepting Secret Santa but now rejecting it while rarely contributing anyway. The user isn't obligated to overspend to accommodate someone who undermines a fair solution. 

The action is financially responsible and respects the prior agreement. It’s not selfish to set boundaries when others are being unreasonable. So, morally acceptable.
